item.title: Where is it more profitable to invest money - in leather bags or AI agents?
item.description:
It seems that the more a developer spends on tokens, the more code they generate with an AI agent, and the faster the project develops. But this is not always the case. Perhaps the code is of such low quality that 90% has to be discarded at the correction stage - so much so that it's easier to write from scratch. However, hiring a developer who will write without AI is also not a guarantee of savings and quality. They solve tasks slowly, make mistakes, and also need to be checked. Who is more profitable to pay: a person or an AI agent? Should the budget be split in half, or is it time to give most of the money to neural networks? To answer these questions, Steffen Herbold from the University of Passau (Germany) built a development model and tested 432 scenarios in search of the most economical team configurations. Spoiler: the dependence of project cost on the proportion of code written with AI is not so simple. But a team where the main part of the budget goes to AI agents is still a long way off. Read more

item.title: AI in Information Security: What Tasks to Automate and Where Human Input is Needed
item.description:
A SOC analyst's morning starts with a queue of alerts: suspicious logins, attempts to access unfamiliar addresses, and triggers from security tools. Some of these are false positives or harmless actions. Each event requires context gathering, root cause analysis, and a decision on intervention. As digital infrastructure evolves, so does the volume and complexity of data. This increases demands on security monitoring, analytics, and incident response tools. In September 2026, Check Point Research recorded an average of 48% more cyberattacks per organization per week compared to September 2025. The ISACA State of Cybersecurity 2026 study found that 52% of surveyed cybersecurity professionals cited excessive workload or unrealistic expectations as a source of stress. The development of automation tools is becoming a key way to improve specialists' efficiency, particularly through artificial intelligence, which aids in analyzing large data volumes, structuring information, and reducing repetitive tasks. At Beeline, the AI Security team is integrating AI into cybersecurity processes to help specialists quickly gather necessary context and focus more on expert tasks. Today, we'll explore where these technologies are already used in the market and how to effectively distribute work between traditional code, AI models, and human analysts.

item.title: How AI Analyzes Logs, Works in Sandboxes, and Saves Tokens. What Was Shown at the Twelfth MWS Meetup
item.description:
AI agents are increasingly gaining access to tools that allow them not only to answer questions but also to perform engineering tasks. They analyze event logs, run code, access services, and independently choose their next actions. However, as these systems become more complex, new questions arise: how to verify the correctness of the model's conclusions, limit its access to infrastructure, and avoid wasting extra tokens on auxiliary operations? At the twelfth MWS meetup, specialists discussed three practical tasks related to the application of AI in development and operations. The first report focused on automatic error diagnostics from logs and traces, the second on isolating agents in Kubernetes, and the third on pre-processing requests using cheaper models. Let's explore the solutions developers are using and the limitations they've encountered.

item.title: How I Invented MCP
item.description:
November. Evening. I'm finishing an article that was supposed to be published in February 2025. It's, to put it mildly, no longer February 2025. The reason is trivial: I don't always have time for my social media. First one project, then another, then a "quick" pet project for the weekend. And now the MCP specification has been updated several times, an official server registry has appeared, and the protocol itself has started to be mentioned in presentations to the board of directors. Spoiler: I didn't invent anything new. I spent two weeks building my version of something that already existed, and found out about it later than I should have. It's called MCP, invented by Anthropic, and I arrived at the same envelope from the other side. This article is not about invention. It's about why it's sometimes useful to be late. Ready-made knowledge answers the question "how." Your own, even if bad, answers the question "why specifically this way." Someone else's protocol, read after your own creation, reads differently: not as an instruction, but as an explanation. I recognized my own solutions and my own dead ends in it. What remains in my head is not a list of points, but a map: what grows from where and where I myself went wrong. This is not an argument for ignorance. Specifications should be read, and the sooner, the cheaper. It's about something else: sometimes it's useful to build your own bicycle first, and then look at the factory one. Not instead of instructions, but before them. The main thing is that the exercise has a timebox, and the creation is not a pity to throw away as soon as the standard appears. Next will be the story of how I hit a wall, built three versions of integration, and in the end found a name for what I had already done. Read more

item.title: Telegram is preparing an AI agent Dictator with access to correspondence and support for local models
item.description:
The agent runs on a separate VPS with Linux, supports plugins, and allows setting permissions for specific actions. We want to know how local this scenario will be in practice. Running an LLM directly on a Mac doesn't mean the entire data processing chain remains local. It's interesting where the agent's memory and task history are stored, what data plugins receive, and what exactly is transmitted to external providers. How Dictator is designed.

item.title: Cloud.ru at AI Journey 2026: Key Takeaways from the Annual International AI Conference
item.description:
From November 26-28, Moscow hosts AI Journey, one of the largest conferences dedicated to artificial intelligence. The event brings together developers, researchers, business representatives, and government officials to discuss the latest AI advancements and showcase practical solutions transforming science, industry, and society. We participated not only by attending sessions but also by presenting new capabilities for working with generative AI: a security architecture, AI budget management tools, and GPU cost-saving technology. Why is this important? Companies want to leverage AI, but face three main barriers: potential data leaks, unpredictable token costs, and expensive, scarce GPUs. We share how we plan to address all three challenges. Read more

item.title: How I Made an LLM Bot That Asks Questions Instead of Giving Answers
item.description:
I'm a database specialist who wanted to try ML for years. I ended up fine-tuning Qwen on coaching club chats, creating a Telegram and VK bot, almost abandoning the project several times, and discovering that teaching a model to ask questions is much easier than teaching it to hold a conversation. This is the story of my first LLM fine-tuning experience, releasing an imperfect product, and trying to figure out if it actually works. Background on Psychology and Coaching I've been familiar with psychology and psychotherapy for a long time – I first saw a psychologist in 2009 when I realized my relationships with people weren't going well. Over the years, I tried different approaches, learned a lot about myself, and then life threw so many challenges my way that I simply didn't have the energy to sort out my internal issues anymore. That's when I found the blog of Lena Sukhareva, a coach with her own signature method – asking 'nasty' questions. They're 'nasty' because they're unpleasant, hit a nerve, and force you to notice your own self-deception, cognitive biases, and other wonderful ways of defending yourself from reality. But it was precisely these questions that unexpectedly helped me look at familiar situations from a different angle. I suddenly remembered that I have my own desires, and for some of them, I don't even need to spend a lot of money; I can just allow myself to fulfill them. Plus, Lena has a club where 'nasty' questions are regularly voiced, and she asks them based on the situations of the women in the club. Read more

item.title: 10 minutes in CAD vs. 3 hours with GPT-6: An experiment with 3D modeling a fan spacer
item.description:
I recently needed a simple plastic spacer to mount a fan for my CPU cooler. Normally, I'd open Tinkercad, spend 5-10 minutes measuring and modeling, and send it to the 3D printer. But I wondered if ChatGPT on the GPT-6 model could do the same based on a technical specification. The result was mixed. We got a working part, but it took about three hours of interaction with the AI instead of 5-10 minutes. Most of that time wasn't even spent modeling. Read on

item.title: Does 'Alice' Dream of Russell's Teapot?
item.description:
The Ministry of Digital Development has published a draft government decree "On Approval of the Rules for Confirming the Compliance of Large Fundamental Artificial Intelligence Models with the Legislation of the Russian Federation and Traditional Russian Spiritual and Moral Values." Once again: this is not a regulation of a public commission at the papacy, not IA "Panorama", it is a draft decree of the country's government, which intends to seriously evaluate AI on a scientific basis for its compliance with the "traditional values" approved by the highest authorities. The confirmation of compliance at the expense of the Ministry of Digital Development's budget will be handled by the FGBC of Science Institute of System Programming named after V.P. Ivannikov RAS. Beware, Anthropic, with your soulless and immoral! Read more

item.title: Higher reasoning effort isn't always better: a benchmark of local LLMs on different thinking levels
item.description:
When working with Claude Code, I intuitively chose the reasoning level for the task type—high for planning, low for code based on a plan, to save tokens. Now I use local models, there are no limits, and we only pay with time: more reasoning tokens mean longer generation. I decided to test my intuition with measurements: I assembled a benchmark of three tasks with traps on a production stack, ran several models at different thinking levels—36 runs isolated in containers. In some measurements, I got results I didn't expect: models were revealed where increasing the reasoning level did not lead to a better outcome. If you are also interested in how much "thinking" a specific local model actually needs to fix bugs, welcome under the cut. Read more
